searchText: Just published a blog-form update on 1559 as it had been requested by a lot of folks in the community: https://hackmd.io/@timbeiko/1559-update-001 I don't think anything in it should be news to most folks here 😅 I expect to keep publishing them every 2-3 weeks. If there's something you'd like to have included in a future update, just ping me about it <@!552133098075193354> I wonder about the value of publishing details about how to get on the implementers call in a community blog post like that. The people we *want* on the call all know how to find it, and the community should definitely have easy access to the recording. Anyone who has legitimate feedback has lots of places they can provide it and if they have valuable feedback that is worthy of bringing up on the call I'm sure someone can/will give them details on how to get to the call. > This indirectly impacts network value by reducing the available supply of ether. <@!552133098075193354> what do you mean with "network value"? Price of ETH? Interesting read that speaks out against burning tokens: https://www.placeholder.vc/blog/2020/9/17/stop-burning-tokens-buyback-and-make-instead So we can think about burning and market-making as two separate operations: (i) remove the tokens from supply, (ii) add tokens to the supply and put them into a market maket This is a useful mental construct because it shows that the question of "burn vs market-make" is really the question of "is issuing into a market maker better than doing nothing"? Which is in turn the question "are the benefits of market making worth the dilution?" To which the answer can only ever be "maybe"! Subsidizing market making is a public good, and as with all public goods, subdizing them is often optimal, though the optimal level is less than infinity So in the case of app tokens, this is maybe a good idea In the case of ETH, the problem is that ethereum the platform does not "trust" any asset other than ETH itself, so.... what does ETH get market-made against? > In the case of ETH, the problem is that ethereum the platform does not "trust" any asset other than ETH itself, so.... what does ETH get market-made against? <@!273808422753796097> I'd see the argument that ETH is market made against bitcoin; that's how it was initially launched @ presale > buybacks do have a positive influence on price, but burning doesn’t create new value, it only redistributes current value among a smaller group of people. There’s a reason why companies that do a lot of buybacks are associated with low growth. ETH can't really be marked made, with proof of stake it is moving more in the direction of a governance token rather than just being a gas mule. The slowed growth potential of burning is what worries me. > I'd see the argument that ETH is market made against bitcoin; that's how it was initially launched @ presale <@!97774605351010304>Bitcoin isn't a trusted asset on Ethereum. Heh, good luck getting the ethereum community to accept bitcoin as an intrinsically privileged asset <@!301186049323958275> lol beat me to it It would require the Ethereum community coming to consensus on a finality time of Bitcoin. 😬 Oh that would be fun actually That sounds like Twitter hell to me. 😛 don't jinx it, now that we have tbtc 😛 We could then over time play the narrative war about how if bitcoin gets 51% attacked, is it *really* clear whether the Nakamoto longest chain or the chain recognized by ethereum are correct, and then over time trojan-horse our way into bitcoin fork choice being based on the ethereum chain, which is something that everyone with WBTC wants because their WBTC is more secure if bitcoin has validity conditions that just make blocks that make invalid-from-ethereum's-perspective withdrawals invalid (jk jk) (Like _that_ isn't going to be taken out of context) I'm certain a screenshot of this conversation with a title "Vitalik wants to take over Bitcoin" is already on Twitter. 😛 > (Like _that_ isn't going to be taken out of context) <@!144468805697929216> At this point I'm happy to just troll 😆 > <@!552133098075193354> I wonder about the value of publishing details about how to get on the implementers call in a community blog post like that. <@!301186049323958275> good point. I removed the link 👍 > <@!552133098075193354> what do you mean with "network value"? Price of ETH? <@!97774605351010304> more like "market cap", but yes, that implies the price of ETH How do you prove that Eip1559 will increase the price? who am i complaining to if it goes down 🤨 We don't "prove" it, but EIP-1559 will decrease the supply, and the amount by which it does so is proportional to usage, given the base fee rises when blocks are full. Obviously, there are many _other_ factors that affect the price of ETH, so it's naive to think the EIP itself will cause the price to rise given that something else of a larger magnitude could affect it more. But your post doesn’t mention any of the other factors but makes it sound like that the EIP by itself will pump the price. Very misleading imo. That's fair. I tried to explain what the feedback mechanism was in detail, but perhaps I should have added an extra caveat? > Finally, burning the BASE FEE creates a positive feedback loop between network usage and network value. As more people want to use the network, the BASE FEE goes up, which means a larger amount of ether gets burnt in each block. This indirectly impacts network value by reducing the available supply of ether. I could add a footnote, around the lines of: > Obviously, many other factors can affect the network value, and ETH has historically been very volatile. There is no guarantee that EIP-1559 would bring network value higher than it is today. And that leads to my next question: Why is that even being used as argument if it depends on X other factors to make that argument valid? There are many „IFs“ and uncertainties with this EIP which i believe many are not aware of. That’s also why i asked if you can prove it. I could also make the point that Eip1559 will crash Eth price. I think that's a bit different though: the burn mechansim _does_ reduce supply, and price is a function of supply and demand. We obviously can't control demand, hence the uncertainty. If you have a valid argument for why 1559 would negatively impact the price of ETH, then it's absolutely something we should consider as a risk and address. Just added a footnote to the post making it clearer, <@!97774605351010304> > If you have a valid argument for why 1559 would negatively impact the price of ETH, then it's absolutely something we should consider as a risk and address. <@!552133098075193354> 0) There might be less usage for ETH because everyone starts speculating about what could happen if the supply decreased even more! <- Yes, this would also require a few factors to line up, just like the "Moon" argument. :) 1) We expect every gateway to implement it flawlessly when for instances exchanges can barely keep up a full node without complaining. What happens if they implement it incorrectly? 2) ETHUSD went from a few dollars to $1500, that's a 30,000% increase without burning anything. What would have happened if EIP1559 was implemented? 3) Miner's could push the BASEFEE to 0. "But that would be equivalent to a 51% attack." No, it is not. 51% attacks are a short term gain, whereas pushing the basefee down would be a longterm gain > 1) We expect every gateway to implement it flawlessly when for instances exchanges can barely keep up a full node without complaining. What happens if they implement it incorrectly? We're currently reaching out to exchanges/gateways to get a feel for what they need to support it. We'll share the aggregated feedback in the next couple weeks as we wrap up interviews. I believe ethernodes has submitted a response already. Also, both legacy and 1559-style txns are anticipated to be supported for a while after the launch of 1559 (how long is going to be informed by those conversations). > 2) ETHUSD went from a few dollars to $1500, that's a 30,000% increase without burning anything. > What would have happened if EIP1559 was implemented? Not sure I understand this? The rise to 1500$ was caused by more demand (ICOs, mostly). Again, 1559 affects supply. > 3) Miner's could push the BASEFEE to 0. "But that would be equivalent to a 51% attack." > No, it is not. 51% attacks are a short term gain, whereas pushing the basefee down would be a longterm gain Can you expand on how they would do that? > Not sure I understand this? The rise to 1500$ was caused by more demand (ICOs, mostly). Again, 1559 affects supply. <@!552133098075193354> maybe, maybe not. Pure speculation. That's why I believe eip1559 is nonsense as it doesn't guarantee anything but puts the whole network at risk I mean, price aside, it does help with processing txns quicker and handling spikes in usage more rapidly. Would you be more in favor of something like 1559 that didn't burn the BASE FEE? > it does help with processing txns quicker how? because you always have extra room in your block, unless there's a sudden spike in demand > something like 1559 that didn't burn the BASE FEE? not really, i'd rather have it in ETH2.0 and bait users with that moon argument to eth2.0 I see a large part of the value of what we're doing now in proving out that this _can_ work for Eth2 (and Eth1 obviously) Eth1 will basically be the 1559 MVP for Eth2 And, if the Eth2 plan still is to have and Eth1 shard as the first one, then we need 1559 in Eth1 to make that happen. And we probably don't want to hard fork both from PoW to PoS *and* to 1559 at the same time 😅 have you done the the calculations how much ETH would be burned if EIP 1559 was implemented asap for the next 3 years (assuming eth2 transition is then) ? Then I'd ask myself if burning X Eth is worth putting the network at risk; or if i would rather wait a few years How would deploying this on Eth2 make things less risky, though? I get the argument that doing nothing is less risky do you actually believe that burning a few M of ETH will push the price? did the parity bug pump the price? lol but IMO waiting until Eth2 and deploying 1559 as part of that transition feels _way_ riskier we have ~10% of the supply in defi, but price is dropping * I mean, the price has roughly tripled over the past 6 mo? Again, I think it's hard to predict or make inferences on the actual price because there are a ton of factors at play, but yes, I suspect if you were to remove the 10% that's held in DeFi today, the price would drop this is literally what we are trying to do before eth2 So do you think we should just not have large protocol changes on Eth1 until Eth2? yep i.e. Account Abstractions, Statlessness/Witnesses, etc. EIP1559 is the first EIP that actually touches the whole protocol, doesnt it ? I'm not sure of the full history, but it definitely is one of the largest if not the single biggest one, yep. I think it's on par with something like adding witnesses in terms of complexity. Because they change the txn format, block header, propagation, etc. there is a difference between actual improvements and speculation, eip1559 is based on speculation. Unless i missed any of the proves you have linked I think EIP-1559 *does* help beyond price: you get better predicability of txn fees, extra space in each block for quick inclusion and process spikes in usage quicker. https://twitter.com/realLedgerwatch/status/1306870150013095936 basically this I really don’t see the point in leaving half the block empty and wasting resources when instead we could work on making it more efficient and increasing throughput. How is forcing a market onto a eip 1559 function more efficient? the average capacity would be the same as today (half empty/half full isn't really the point here). The max block size increases to up to 2x current size The fee market is incredibly inefficient and a usability nightmare today. Vitalik's FAQ is on 1559
